Recurring reference performance tests and EIS measurements track the evolution of each cell. Teardown data were obtained from pristine and aged (post-mortem) cells. They include material analyses and half-cell measurements. This single dataset supports analytics, model development (both machine-learning and physics-based), benchmarking, and techno-economic analysis. Several example analyses are carried out to show the usability of the data. For instance, the paper shows how lithium stripping can be detected from the voltage response of a short discharge applied after each charge. The data and the processing and analysis scripts are openly provided alongside this paper.

title: The Loss or the Architecture? What Matters in Survival Analysis with Competing Risks
summary: Often, \emph{eg} in healthcare and predictive maintenance, what matters is which of several competing causes will strike first, and with what probability: survival analysis with competing risks. Corresponding deep learning methods are developed as bundles: a new architecture together with a new training loss, tested on one to five datasets against a handful of baselines. Thus, a state-of-the-art result cannot be attributed to the architecture, the loss, or the evaluation protocol. The coupling is not accidental: with one incidence curve per cause, a network's head is tied to the losses expressible on it. We vary the two axes independently, three losses, two of them strictly proper, on four backbones, across two modalities that tease the axes apart: 20 tabular and 3 pathology-image datasets. One loss wins in both: modelling cumulative incidence directly under censoring weighting. It brings twice as much as benefits a good choice of backbone on competing-risks data, and no more than it on single-event data: the loss is decisive for competing risks. The backbone matters too, and must match the modality: tabular networks lead on tables, pretrained vision encoders on images. The two choices compound rather than substitute. Proper scoring rules reveal these dynamics; the concordance index (C-index), which is not proper, does not separate models: neither axis moves it, not even tuning on the loss built to improve it. This is an avenue of progress: composed, the two give a model nobody has tried, RealMLP or TabM trained with the cumulative-incidence loss, which takes the best Brier score in our benchmark.

title: Covert Digital Semantic Communication With Movable Antennas: Constellation Shaping, Spatial Optimization, and Semantic Mapping
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications (JSAC)
summary: Digital semantic communication (SemCom) is emerging as a bandwidth-efficient paradigm for next-generation wireless networks by delivering the meaning of a source over finite constellations. However, the broadcast nature of wireless channels exposes transmissions to adversarial wardens, while discrete symbols deviate from the Gaussian signaling assumed by conventional covert communication. In this paper, we propose a covert digital SemCom system assisted by movable antennas (MAs), where the constellation, the antenna positions, and the semantic transceiver are jointly designed to conceal the transmission while preserving the semantic fidelity. Specifically, the maximum covert rate against the optimal detector with unknown noise level is derived in closed-form, which reveals that the legitimate signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) scales with the moment-matching order of the constellation and the spatial gain provided by the MA array. A Gauss-Laguerre ring constellation is then designed to raise the moment-matching order under the peak power constraints, and a covert symbol mapping with rank-to-ring assignment and scrambling is developed to carry the semantics in the ordering of the latent magnitudes. Guided by the derived semantic distortion bound, the semantic encoder and decoder are trained end-to-end through an invertible flow over the designed constellation and MA array. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme supports a higher achievable covert rate and improves the reconstruction quality by 24% compared to state-of-the-art SemCom schemes.

title: Testing Treatment Effect Heterogeneity with Functional Outcomes
comment: 24 pages. Includes brief proof outlines; detailed technical proofs and supplementary numerical/empirical appendices are not included in this preprint version
summary: Assessing treatment-effect heterogeneity is important in causal inference, particularly for functional outcomes where effects may vary over time and the common effect is unknown. We propose a nonparametric procedure that assesses treatment-effect homogeneity through a testable marginal implication. By comparing within-arm difference distributions, the construction removes the unknown common functional effect without estimating it. We measure departures between these distributions through an integrated squared discrepancy of their characteristic functionals. A full-support Gaussian integrating measure yields an explicit bounded-kernel representation and identifies equality of the difference laws without requiring moment conditions on the outcomes. We construct an unbiased generalized U-statistic that accounts for dependence among overlapping differences, derive its null, fixed-alternative, and local-alternative limits, and develop a centered multiplier bootstrap for inference. The framework extends to multiple treatment arms with a shared control. For computation, a random-direction approximation combined with a nine-state recursion reduces the cost to linear order in the sample size for fixed numerical settings. Simulation studies assess the finite-sample performance of the proposed procedure relative to several benchmark methods. An application to the Irish gas smart-metering trial illustrates its use for assessing heterogeneity in functional treatment responses.

title: LWMa: Distributed Deployment of an Angle-Delay-Domain Wireless Foundation Model for Multiple Tasks
summary: The growing diversity of wireless services in sixth-generation (6G) wireless communication systems calls for reusable channel representations that support multiple tasks across different propagation environments. However, deploying such representations between user equipment and the base station in frequency-division duplexing systems faces uplink feedback constraints. This paper proposes a distributed framework based on an angle-delay-domain large wireless model (LWMa) for multiple tasks. LWMa exploits angle-delay structure and delay truncation to improve feature extraction and reduce computational cost. A scenario-specific network inspired by Perceiver IO (input-output) compresses embeddings for channel reconstruction tasks, while other tasks use a low-dimensional compact global embedding. Embedding reconstruction training followed by channel-quality-guided fine-tuning preserves information useful for downstream processing. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed method supports effective channel reconstruction and multiple tasks under limited feedback with reduced deployment complexity. Further evaluations show that the recovered embeddings generalize to additional tasks and support split inference.

title: Closely spaced change-point detection with an application to geopolitical shocks in oil and gas markets
summary: Change points that arrive in quick succession, or near the boundaries of the sample, are prone to type-II error: the few observations trapped between successive breaks carry too little information for global procedures to analyze. This article develops a test statistic, $I_1$, for which we derive the limiting null distribution under Gaussian noise, extend the theory to weakly dependent sequences, and prove consistency under a mean-shift alternative. Around $I_1$, we construct DCI, a two-phase algorithm that couples a global scan with multiple local tests via an adaptive-width sliding window. In extensive simulations, $I_1$ and DCI remain Pareto-optimal over criteria spaces spanning true and false positive rates, localization error, and segmentation covering. An application to the US-Iran 2026 conflict quantifies the exposure of energy markets to geopolitical shocks using two new metrics, event sensitivity and event attribution, leading to time series tokenization.

title: Spatiotemporal Adaptive Eigenspectrum Remapping in Transcranial Ultrasound Localization Microscopy
summary: Clutter suppression is a critical preprocessing step in ultrasound blood flow imaging, yet conventional singular value decomposition (SVD) filtering depends on data-specific eigenvalue cutoffs that can remove slow flow along with tissue clutter. Here, we introduce adaptive eigenspectrum remapping (AER), a general framework in which clutter is suppressed by continuously remapping, rather than truncating, the eigenvalue spectrum of the spatiotemporal covariance, and we investigate zero-phase component analysis (ZCA) matrix whitening as an instance of AER for transcranial ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM). Rather than discarding eigenspaces, ZCA-based AER whitens the eigenvalue spectrum, reducing the dominance of coherent clutter, including skull reverberation, while retaining weak flow signals. We evaluate AER on both temporal and spatial covariance matrices in mouse brain datasets acquired with long temporal ensembles. Compared with SVD filtering, ZCA improves microbubble contrast and vascular image quality, increases trajectory density across low- and high-concentration regimes, and reveals more low-velocity trajectories in ULM velocity maps. Spatial AER further maintains reconstruction quality across extended ensembles and enables fuller single capillary reporter (SCaRe) reconstructions, including connected artery-to-capillary-to-vein tracks. These results support AER, here instantiated as ZCA whitening, as a data-adaptive alternative to manually thresholded SVD filtering for high-resolution microvascular imaging.

title: Towards optimal selection schedules for online active learning
summary: We consider the problem of online linear classification, where a stream of unlabeled samples is available, and annotation is costly. We investigate the optimal query policy, that prescribes whether and when a sample should be labeled and used for a training step, or instead discarded, so as to minimize a given objective. We focus on the realizable case, under Gaussian design, in the high-dimensional regime where data dimension and number of unlabeled samples grow proportionally. We consider two objectives: 1) the generalization error under a labeling budget, and 2) a cumulative cost function where mistakes have unit cost and queries cost $Δ$. We first show that the myopic policies that greedily minimize at all times the increment in the objective correspond to either small or intermediate-margin policies, that prescribe the selection of samples whose margins fall within certain intervals that shrink with time. Within this class, we numerically ascertain the optimal schedules for the selection thresholds that minimize the final values of the objectives. Taking inspiration from the myopic policy for the cumulative cost, we design a very simple query policy schedule that we compare to other proposed heuristics, on synthetic data and real medical image datasets. Finally, we discuss myopic policies for two-layer neural networks, and exemplify how naive margin-based policies can cease to be optimal.

title: Keep Pace to Learn: Movable Antennas Restore the Backpropagated Gradient Under User Mobility
summary: When a mobile terminal takes part in over-the-air training, its own motion rotates the gradient that travels back through it; a movable antenna that keeps pace with the terminal rotates it back---without any channel estimate. We give a speed law: under a scalar conditional-mean model of the physical return, landing the residual displacement inside the first positive lobe of the spatial correlation keeps the conditional mean gradient a descent direction, which, given sufficient travel, fixes a critical actuator-to-terminal speed ratio. We further prove a bias--jitter law: under the same scalar conditional-mean model and with zero effective bias, independent zero-mean Gaussian jitter of any finite amplitude scales the conditional mean gradient without reversing its direction, whereas a sub-wavelength systematic bias can reverse it. This result motivates prioritizing bias calibration to preserve gradient direction. Simulations on 3GPP CDL-A channels show that an antenna keeping pace with the terminal achieves near-CSI accuracy without digital channel correction, reaching 98.58 % compared with 98.59% for the ideal-CSI reference. The simulations also show that partial compensation can support learning when the residual displacement falls within a later positive correlation lobe, so a faster actuator does not necessarily yield higher accuracy. Separate positioning simulations show a sharp accuracy loss under systematic bias but little degradation under zero-mean Gaussian jitter of comparable spatial scale.

title: Scaling Spatially Varying Distributed Lag Nonlinear Models for Nationwide Small-Area Data: A Divide-and-Conquer Approach
summary: Lagged and nonlinear exposure-response relationships are frequently modelled using distributed lag non-linear models (DLNMs). However, these relationships can vary substantially across locations due to differences in climate, population structure, adaptation and socio-economic characteristics, among others. Spatially-varying DLNMs can capture this heterogeneity, but their computational demands limit their application to fine-scale nationwide datasets with thousands of small areas. In this paper, we adapt a 'divide-and-conquer' approach to spatially varying DLNMs. The method partitions the spatial domain into smaller regions, expands each region with a k-order neighbourhood to reduce boundary effects, fits separate models within each partition using Laplacian P-splines, and combines the resulting estimates using conditional predictive ordinate-based mixture weights. We evaluated the approach in a simulation study based on municipalities in Sicily and applied it to daily summer temperature and mortality data from 7122 municipalities in mainland Italy between 2011 and 2021. Simulation studies show good performance, with relative-risk estimates comparable to those from a global model and relatively robust to the choice and number of partitioning units. Computational efficiency can be substantially improved by using parallel computations. The Italian application reveals significant spatial heterogeneity in the temperature-mortality relationship, with clear regional differences. The proposed framework makes spatially varying DLNMs feasible for large, fine-scale spatiotemporal datasets while retaining location-specific exposure-lag-response estimation.

title: Wait to Learn: Lobes and Dead Zones in Physical Backpropagation over an Aging Single-Antenna Channel
summary: Sometimes the best way to correct an aged gradient is to wait. In physical backpropagation, a receiver returns its loss gradient through the reciprocal channel. With a single moving antenna, the mean gradient returned at the antenna is the true one counter-rotated by the phase of the temporal correlation. In simulation, uncorrected training fails in negative correlation lobes and revives in positive ones. At correlation zeros the return is independent of the forward channel, so no linear correction has a mean to recover; near them, more calibration barely helps, but holding the return until the next correlation extremum does.

title: Weighted spatial averages with missing observations: Convergence and accuracy of delta-method variance approximations
summary: Weighted spatial averages from incomplete networks are ratios whose variance is approximated by truncating a Taylor series (the delta method). Three questions remain open: whether the series converges, how large a truncation's error is, and how it behaves as the network grows. We address these for observations missing completely at random, independently with a common probability $α$. First, the truncations, which count corrections for the denominator (the total reported weight) and for its coupling with the numerator, converge for a given network only if $α>\tfrac12$ and both corrections increase together. Second, whether or not the series converges, the error of truncations correcting only for the denominator is controlled at any network size by its coefficient of variation $ρ$, with $ρ^2=\tfrac{1-α}α\sum_iβ_i^2$ for weights $β_i$, and by the probability of rare reporting patterns. Third, for uniform weights and bounded fields, these errors vanish as the network grows, at any fixed availability. If correlations also decay with distance, the first-order approximation of earlier work has error of order $ρ^4$, against $ρ^2$ for the simplest approximation. Only truncations of equal order in numerator and denominator, beginning with the first-order truncation, avoid spurious dependence on the mean level; higher ones need not be more accurate. The exact variance for uniform weights, a single sum, shows that for correlated fields the first-order approximation overstates the contribution of missing data but is conservative overall. Concentrated weights degrade it more than $ρ$ indicates. Rainfall simulations over India illustrates results, several of which extend to self-normalized estimators.

title: Coherent but Discordant: Rotate, Don't Invert, to Backpropagate Through an Aging Channel
summary: A channel can be almost perfectly coherent and still teach a transmitter the wrong direction. In physical ("over-the-air") backpropagation, the receiver sends its loss gradient back through the reciprocal channel; when the terminal moves in between, mobility does not merely add noise to the returned gradient, it rotates it. Under a scalar conditional mean model the rotation is set by the phase of the temporal correlation, so coherence, which measures only its magnitude, is the wrong ruler: in simulation, channels with absolute value of rho greater than 0.9 drive uncorrected training to 51.7% accuracy, while phase correction restores 92.5%. Arrays add a twist. Near zeros of the trace correlation, scalar correction fails even with rho known exactly, yet most of the information is still there: noise has moved it onto neighbouring antennas. Re-indexing the ports by the displacement, with zero digital feedback, recovers the lost performance in simulation, and so does rotating the returned seed with the unitary polar factor of the conditional mean operator, never inverting it; aligning each antenna's phase with its own past makes things worse. An exact array identity explains all three. The lesson fits in one line: correct the rotation, not the stretch.

title: Adaptive conformal prediction on the Grassmannian
summary: We introduce a conformal prediction framework for regression with Grassmann-valued responses. The proposed method constructs prediction regions in the form of metric balls directly on the Grassmann manifold, using basis-invariant geometric distances as non-conformity measures and scaling the corresponding non-conformity scores through a learned prediction difficulty estimator. This yields locally adaptive, input-dependent prediction regions that respect the underlying manifold geometry, while retaining the finite-sample marginal coverage guarantee of split conformal prediction under exchangeability. We evaluate several Grassmannian distance metrics and compare their prediction-region efficiency on synthetic benchmarks and an airfoil inverse shape-design problem. The results highlight the advantages of geometry-aware non-conformity scores, while local adaptation improves empirical coverage uniformity across prediction difficulty levels and, in strongly heteroscedastic settings, can substantially reduce prediction-region size while maintaining the target coverage.

title: Robust Design of Sensing-Assisted Secure Transmission for RIS-Aided ISAC System under Eavesdropper 3D Positioning Uncertainty
summary: Localization errors in estimating the position of a potential eavesdropper (Eve) pose a critical challenge to secure transmission in reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems. To address this issue, this paper proposes a sensing-assisted robust secure transmission framework that exploits ISAC sensing to characterize the positioning uncertainty induced by these errors. The RIS is partitioned into a reflection region and a sensing reception region, supporting sensing and communication through spatial separation. By jointly exploiting observations collected at the base station (BS) and the RIS sensing reception region, maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) is employed to estimate the arrival angles, from which Eve's three-dimensional (3D) position is obtained through cross localization. The resulting localization Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB) is then used to construct an ellipsoidal uncertainty region around the estimated position. A two-stage optimization strategy is developed. In Stage I, the sensing beamformer and RIS reflection coefficients are jointly optimized to improve localization accuracy. In Stage II, the resulting positioning uncertainty is incorporated into a robust secure transmission design, where the communication beamformer and RIS reflection coefficients are jointly optimized to maximize the worst-case secrecy rate. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms benchmark schemes without RIS assistance and with random RIS configurations in terms of secrecy performance. The proposed framework effectively mitigates secrecy performance degradation caused by localization errors in Eve's position.

title: Causal Discovery beyond Conditional Independence: Identifiability, Algorithms, and Statistical Inference for Directed Acyclic and Cyclic Graphs
summary: Learning causal structure from data requires assumptions about mechanisms, noises, observation schemes, and interventions. Historically, causal discovery has relied primarily on conditional independence. This review focuses on modern causal discovery methods that exploit properties of distributions beyond conditional independence. Our organizing principle separates the source of identification from the statistical estimator and its computational implementation. This perspective connects conditional-independence methods with distributional asymmetries, conditional-moment restrictions, and variation across environments or individuals. We examine discovery under latent confounding and feedback, distinguishing causal information about observed variables from reconstruction of latent structure and emphasizing the additional semantics required by cyclic models. We also distinguish population identification, frequentist and Bayesian consistency, uncertainty quantification, and algorithmic guarantees. Throughout, examples show why the same observational distribution can support different conclusions under different model classes. We conclude with guidance for comparing methods at their identifiable targets and a research agenda for uncertainty, heterogeneous populations, non-scalar variables, and the intersection of discrete data, feedback, and hidden confounding.

title: Entropy-Based Wireless Technology Recognition
summary: Wireless Technology Recognition (WTR) enables identifying wireless technologies from received radio signals and is important for spectrum monitoring and management systems. Existing approaches either rely on handcrafted signal features with limited robustness or computationally intensive Deep Learning (DL) models operating on high-dimensional In-phase and Quadrature (IQ) samples or spectrograms. In this paper, we investigate a different hypothesis: wireless technologies can be distinguished through the temporal evolution of their local time-frequency complexity. To capture this behavior, we propose a lightweight WTR framework based on two-dimensional dispersion entropy. Entropy values are extracted from successive spectrogram regions to characterize the evolution of local spectrogram complexity throughout a transmission and summarized into a compact feature representation for classification using a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP). The framework is evaluated on seven wireless technologies, namely IEEE 802.11ah, IEEE 802.15.4 SUN-FSK, IEEE 802.15.4 SUN-OFDM, LoRa, IEEE 802.11n, LTE, and 5G NR, at Signal-to-Noise Ratios (SNRs) ranging from -20 dB to 40 dB. Experimental results show that the proposed approach consistently outperforms IQ-based and Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT)-based Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) baselines, particularly at low and moderate SNRs. Averaged across all evaluated SNR levels, it achieves 82.73% accuracy, corresponding to improvements of 23.8% and 14.6% over the IQ-based and STFT-based CNN approaches, respectively. Furthermore, the approach maintains its recognition advantage with data-augmented training while requiring substantially shorter training times. The results demonstrate that temporal evolution of local spectrogram complexity provides a robust technology-specific fingerprint and an effective, computationally efficient representation for WTR.

title: A general recipe for data-adaptive anytime-valid envelopes for iterative algorithms
summary: Most convergence guarantees for iterative stochastic algorithms are stated at a fixed iteration count and do not justify stopping at a data-dependent time. Recent work has constructed anytime-valid envelopes that do, but deterministic envelopes are typically too conservative for practical stopping, and existing data-adaptive ones are derived case-by-case, each coupling a specific algorithm to a specific noise model and boundary construction. This paper provides a general recipe for constructing such anytime-valid data-adaptive boundaries for a large class of iterative algorithms. Performance measures of many of these algorithms satisfy a one-step recursion that reduces the entire error analysis to a single general requirement: time-uniform concentration for predictably weighted sums of noise. We formalize this through a strongly adapted sub-$ψ$ condition, and derive off-the-shelf boundary constructions via continuous and discrete mixtures, stitching, and product betting martingales. We show how these boundaries can be directly coupled with a separate algorithmic analysis that derives the one-step recursion to provide a class of readymade anytime-valid envelopes across diverse settings including stochastic gradient descent (SGD), temporal difference learning, and Bures-Wasserstein SGD. In particular, for SGD, our framework either recovers or significantly sharpens every existing envelope we are aware of. Our constructions come with explicit implementation details and are substantiated by numerical experiments.

title: IMU-Aided Motion Compensation of RSS Measurements for Dynamic Visible Light-Inertial Localization
summary: Visible Light Positioning (VLP) offers high-precision indoor positioning using existing LED infrastructure. However, in VLP systems using Photodiodes (PDs) as receivers, rapid movement of the PD causes measurement inaccuracies as the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) processing yields averaged rather than instantaneous Received Signal Strength (RSS) values. To address this challenge, we propose an RSS correction algorithm that integrates Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) data with VLP observations to compensate for motion-induced distortions. Our approach leverages IMU-derived motion parameters to model the temporal variation of optical signals during the DFT window, enabling instantaneous RSS estimation. The algorithm is embedded within both tightly and simply coupled VLP/INS integration frameworks that estimate the pose of the moving receiver. This work targets highly dynamic indoor navigation. Simulations validate the correction model, and total-station-tracked experiments confirm reduced RSS discrepancies against model references. Across eight held-out high-dynamic handheld trials with peak translational and angular speeds of 2.25 m/s and 284 deg/s, correction reduces the pooled 3D position and PD-normal inclination root mean square errors relative to the LiDAR/IMU reference with a shared IMU by 56.0% and 71.9%, respectively. Both datasets and source code are publicly available.

title: A Bayesian model averaging approach for estimating longitudinal treatment effects
summary: Several methods have been proposed for performing variable selection for the goal of estimating the average treatment effect of a point treatment on an outcome. Much less work has focused on developing methods for performing variable selection when the goal is instead to estimate the causal effect of a longitudinal treatment on an outcome. We introduce a Bayesian model averaging approach to estimate counterfactual means under longitudinal treatment regimes as well as the parameters of longitudinal marginal structural models. The Bayesian model averaging framework provides a principled way to produce valid post-selection inference. We further devise an informative prior distribution that favors the selection of optimal adjustment sets, in the sense that the resulting estimator has the lowest possible variance among all possible adjustment sets. We show through simulation results that our proposed method outperforms fully adjusted estimators and even performs similarly to an oracle estimator in several scenarios. In a real-data illustration, our method yields estimates with markedly reduced standard errors for the effect of cumulative exposure to statins for the prevention of a first cardiovascular disease or death among older adults.

title: Distributed Performance Boosting through Neural Control for Plug-and-Play Networks
summary: We address the problem of improving the performance of pre-stabilized networked systems subject to plug-and-play (PnP) operations, namely additions or removals of subsystems. While distributed baseline controllers can preserve stability after a PnP transition, augmenting them with expressive neural policies can invalidate the formal stability guarantees. To overcome this issue, we build on recently proposed Performance Boosting controllers based on the Internal Model Control (IMC) principle, which reduce closed-loop stability to a finite $\ell_2$-gain requirement on an auxiliary operator. In the distributed setting, this operator is formed by interconnecting local neural operators that exchange information only between neighboring subsystems. We then derive free parametrizations of this interconnection, namely explicit maps from unconstrained trainable variables to interconnected neural operators satisfying a prescribed network gain bound for every parameter value. The obtained distributed neural controller can therefore be trained by unconstrained gradient-based optimization without stability constraints or projection steps, while retaining the prescribed gain bound at every training iterate. We develop two complementary parametrizations. A neighbor-based compositional parametrization uses local coupling bounds, so that after a PnP event only subsystems whose bounds change need to update their gain parameters. A network-norm parametrization instead uses a bound on the overall coupling matrix and can reduce conservatism, at the price of requiring network-wide information. A PnP DC-microgrid case study shows that the proposed neural layer improves voltage transients under topology changes and load variations while preserving nominal closed-loop stability.

title: Exact Tail Laws for Nonlinear SGD with Infinite-Variance Gradients
summary: With infinite-variance gradient noise, SGD can have infinite expected excess objective even when most iterates are close to the optimum. We characterize its accuracy through exact first-order tail probabilities for the last iterate of nonlinear, constant-stepsize SGD. For regularly varying innovations of index $t\in(1,2)$, the leading measure transports one large gradient shock through the local Hessian flow. This is the same measure that governs the central stable Ornstein--Uhlenbeck limit; we prove its relative accuracy at shrinking tolerances above the central scale, with state-dependent noise and a growing observation horizon. The admissible window is nonempty for every available gradient moment $p>1$. The main technical step is a moment bound at the central fluctuation scale and a lower-moment control of the nonlinear error. The result yields explicit projection and excess-objective tails, extreme quantiles, and a factor $b^{1-t}$ for fixed batch size $b$. For affine population gradients, a sharper comparison gives the same law at fixed tolerances, including random sample Hessians. Coupled simulations in dimensions one to one hundred examine relative calibration, objective quantiles, batch effects, and the error due to random curvature.

title: TransNSNet: A Transformer-Enhanced Multi-Scale Adversarial Framework for CT-to-PET Image Synthesis
comment: 21 pages, 7 figures. Supplementary material included. Under review at Biomedical Signal Processing and Control
summary: This study investigates CT-to-PET image synthesis using TransNSNet, a Transformer-enhanced multi-scale adversarial framework. A paired CT-PET dataset was curated from the public non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) Radiogenomics collection through patient screening, slice-level matching, preprocessing, and patient-level train-test separation. The proposed framework generates PET-like predictions at multiple spatial scales and applies coarse-to-fine reconstruction supervision, while TransPatchGAN introduces contextual feature interaction into adversarial evaluation. A progressive ablation study compares Pix2Pix, NSNet-Base, NSNet-D, and TransNSNet. Image-level performance was summarized over a fixed convergence window (epochs 80-101) from one training run per model. TransNSNet achieved the best mean value in nine of ten metrics, whereas NSNet-Base achieved the highest visual saliency-induced index. For fixed-fraction high-intensity regions, NSNet-D was marginally higher in slice-level recall and balanced accuracy, but the equal-weight patient-level values were nearly identical and the highest Dice values shifted to TransNSNet. These differences were small relative to between-patient variability. In the separate adaptive patient-level analysis (n=10), no pairwise model difference remained statistically significant after Holm correction. TransNSNet also had a substantially smaller parameter footprint than the original next-scale models. These findings indicate promising image-quality trends, but they do not establish statistical superiority or clinical validity; synthesized PET-like images should not be interpreted as substitutes for clinically acquired PET.

title: Robust Local Fréchet Regression: Nonasymptotic Theory and Minimax Optimality
comment: 62 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Includes supplementary material
summary: We develop robust local Fréchet regression for heavy-tailed responses in a general metric space and propose a distance-based median-of-means estimator. We derive nonasymptotic pointwise high-probability bounds separately under local second-order smoothness and local $1$-Wasserstein Hölder continuity, and show that the corresponding optimized rates match the classical pointwise rates for nonparametric regression. We also establish matching pointwise minimax lower bounds over embedded Gaussian regression subclasses. Remarkably, our results do not require an entropy condition on the response space. Simulation studies with positive-definite matrix-valued responses, together with a real-data application involving Wasserstein-valued responses, illustrate the robustness--efficiency tradeoff and practical performance of the proposed estimator.

title: Structured Authority Injection: Persistent Human Control for LLM Agents via Typed MCP Overrides
summary: LLM-based agents are increasingly used as autonomous orchestrators in distributed and multi-agent systems, yet a control gap remains: no protocol-level mechanism allows human operators to inject binding directives that persist across planning cycles. Free-text overrides suffer from ambiguous interpretation due to lack of schema validation and from authority erosion as operator instructions lose influence within accumulating context. We propose Structured Authority Injection (SAI), a protocol that addresses these issues by routing operator corrections through typed, schema-validated Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool calls and maintaining a ranked authority context prepended to each LLM prompt. SAI defines three override classes (Constraint, Priority, and Strategy) with distinct persistence semantics and an explicit precedence order enforced via a directed authority channel inaccessible to the planning process. The method requires no model fine-tuning or access to model weights and applies to instruction-tuned LLMs supporting MCP tool use. Evaluation across nine LLMs and eight scenarios targeting agent failure modes shows reduced ambiguous directive interpretation and mitigated authority decay across planning iterations, with lower prompt overhead in the strongest models (up to 38% depending on model and scenario), though benefit varies substantially across models. SAI provides a general design pattern for agent systems requiring explicit and persistent human control.

title: Joint Subcarrier and Power Allocation for Localization-Oriented Multi-Carrier Underwater ISAC Systems
summary: Multi-carrier underwater integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) realizes concurrent acoustic communication and localization, yet the frequency selectivity of the acoustic channel creates uneven positioning capabilities across subcarriers. This paper proposes a localization-oriented subcarrier and power allocation scheme for multi-anchor underwater ISAC systems. We build a unified orthogonal subcarrier multiplexing framework and derive closed-form Cramer-Rao bounds (CRBs) under frequency-selective channels with colored noise. We derive a subcarrier-level localization information contribution from the time of arrival Fisher information, which enables localization-oriented resource allocation. We derive several theoretical properties regarding the distance and frequency dependence of the localization information metric, and establish a distance-frequency matching principle. These results provide a theoretical foundation for localization-oriented resource allocation and guide the design of a low-complexity greedy algorithm that improves positioning accuracy. Specifically, the algorithm iteratively allocates subcarriers to minimize the residual positioning-error objective, thereby improving positioning accuracy while satisfying communication quality-of-service (QoS) constraints. Simulations verify that our method yields much lower positioning error bound than uniform, random and high-frequency-first subcarrier allocation in symmetric or asymmetric topologies while guaranteeing communication QoS, achieving superior communication-localization tradeoffs.

title: Mesoscopic learning dynamics of extensive-width neural networks
summary: Understanding how stochastic gradient descent learns internal representations in wide neural networks trained on rich target functions is a central problem in machine learning. We study this question in two-layer neural networks learning target functions represented by networks of the same architecture, with arbitrary nonlinearity, and with network width and input dimension growing proportionally. In this regime, standard approaches for describing the learning dynamics require tracking a diverging number of overlaps, which measure correlations between learned and target features, leaving no obvious description in terms of a few order parameters. Here, we develop a mesoscopic description of learning by characterizing the distribution of overlaps. In the early stages of learning, we find that a Gaussian description of overlap statistics reduces the learning dynamics to a few collective variables that track learning of the target function's linear and quadratic components. We then estimate the timescale of specialization, when Gaussian closure breaks down and individual learned features begin to strongly correlate with specific target features. We find that specialization in extensive-rank networks is accelerated via a quadratic shielding mechanism, whereby learning the linear and quadratic components of the target function filters gradient fluctuations. We finally describe how the activation function determines the pattern of specialization and characterize the subsequent refinement of learned features. Together, these results show how collective learning gives way to individual feature discovery and clarify when learning in large neural networks admits a simple statistical description.

title: Memory Bandwidth, Not FLOPs: Profiling and Accelerating Query-Based Segmentation Decoders on Edge GPUs
comment: Accepted at the British Machine Vision Conference (BMVC) 2026. Supplementary material included
summary: Query-based segmentation models achieve strong performance even under real-time inference on workstation GPUs. On edge devices, however, we show their transformer decoders are deeply memory-bandwidth-bound, a bottleneck invisible to standard FLOP analysis that worsens with input resolution and limited DRAM bandwidth. An FP16 roofline analysis with tensor-core GEMMs active and hardware DRAM counters shows that the non-tensor-core aggregates of FastInst and Mask2Former reach only $2.5\%$ to $6\%$ of the CUDA-core ridge yet account for $53\%$ to $70\%$ of decoder time and $61\%$ to $71\%$ of decoder bytes. The largest individual kernels sustain up to $90\%$ of nominal peak DRAM bandwidth, effectively saturating the memory bus. The bottleneck is therefore not primarily low GEMM intensity, but cross-kernel activation traffic. CompactInst addresses this bottleneck using parameter-free spatial pooling at $4{\times}$, which reduces the bytes moved within the transformer decoder, while a two-convolution refinement head recovers spatial detail. Under TensorRT FP16 on Jetson Orin Nano, CompactInst delivers decoder speedups from $2.35{\times}$ to $4.74{\times}$ and model speedups from $1.57{\times}$ to $2.62{\times}$ as input resolution grows, while closely matching accuracy ($-0.4$ AP on COCO val2017, $+0.2$ AP on Cityscapes test). A heavier variant with $2.57{\times}$ more decoder FLOPs still runs its decoder $1.74{\times}$ faster on the most bandwidth-constrained device, confirming at the deployment level that decoder bytes, not FLOPs, govern latency.

title: AWM: An All-in-One Wireless Foundation Model for Multi-User Channel Acquisition and Localization Without Downstream Tuning
summary: Wireless foundation models (WFMs) seek to unify diverse wireless tasks and scenarios, yet existing methods still rely on task- or scenario-specific components or deployment-time fine-tuning. This paper presents an all-in-one wireless model (AWM), a WFM that unifies multi-user channel acquisition and localization, despite their distinct data modalities and functional objectives. We reveal that user location and channel state information (CSI) at different frequencies can be viewed as attribute-specific measurements of the same wireless link. By introducing in-scenario same-attribute reference pairs as prompts, AWM converts heterogeneous attributes into alignable relativity representations, formulating intra-band channel interpolation, inter-band channel prediction, and wireless localization as unified wireless-state transformations. Further, a multi-task MateFormer is developed to perform source-attribute relativity extraction, cross-attribute relativity alignment, and target-attribute synthesis within a unified architecture, avoiding task-specific output heads or downstream fine-tuning. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of model unification, including substantial gains from cross-task knowledge sharing, seamless generalization to unseen scenarios, and an efficient closed-loop service for mobile users.

title: Feasible closed form moment matching for scenario generation through covariance rotations
summary: Closed form moment matching constructs small scenario sets without numerical optimisation. We study two generators that match the mean, the covariance matrix, and the marginal third and fourth moments. Both place their scenarios along the columns of a covariance factor, usually the symmetric or Cholesky root. Although every valid factor reproduces the same covariance matrix, its choice can determine whether the resulting weights are nonnegative. By viewing each column as a univariate mixture component, Pearson's inequality gives the minimum probability needed to reproduce its assigned variance, skewness, and kurtosis, which leads to exact feasibility conditions whenever the relevant entrywise powers are nonsingular. The effect of the factor is governed by its entrywise fourth powers, whose sum can vary by a factor equal to the dimension. This explains why standard roots fail in high dimension. We combine these results into a rotated moment matching procedure that searches for feasible factors without altering the target moments. Applied to stock returns and synthetic data, the procedure produces valid probabilities for both generators in nearly every instance considered, and it outperforms the original constructions, whose standard factors give invalid weights in most of them. Finally, the two asset case explains when such a rotation exists. With symmetric marginals, a suitable rotation reaches Pearson's bound except in one degenerate case, whereas with skewness the factor must balance the allocation of third and fourth moments, and some attainable targets admit no feasible rotation. We also establish a sufficient condition for arbitrary correlation and equal marginal kurtosis.

title: When is a large language model a good calibration agent? Physics-labeled prompting for budgeted engineering simulator calibration
comment: Submitted to Engineering Application of Artificial Intelligence
summary: Calibrating expensive engineering simulators requires tuning model parameters to match reference data, a process heavily constrained by computational costs. This study investigates whether Large Language Models (LLMs), conditioned on physical diagnostic descriptions of simulation errors, can propose informative parameter updates more efficiently than conventional derivative-free optimizers. We test this on a cylinder-wake Large-Eddy Simulation and a damped-oscillator inverse problem. Physics-labeled prompts are evaluated against four text ablations (removed, anonymized, padded, misdirected) and standard optimizers (Nelder-Mead, Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, and random search). Results demonstrate a strong early semantic advantage: the first physics-informed LLM proposal improves the initial design in 23 of 25 trials. After five evaluations, the median calibration error is 21.9 times lower than physics-free controls. However, this advantage is transient - disappearing by fifteen evaluations - and inherent LLM decoder variability yields a 9.8-fold performance spread. To address this, we introduce a hybrid workflow that uses the LLM as a warm-start, passing accumulated evaluations to a conventional optimizer. This two-stage numerical continuation policy reaches target accuracy in just 9 simulator runs, outperforming the LLM alone (12 runs), Nelder-Mead (17 runs), and Bayesian optimization (>60 runs). Supported by sensitivity analysis validating the test cases, this hybrid physics-labeled LLM scheme proves highly effective as a calibration agent under strict evaluation budgets.

title: Pilot-Based Sensing With OFDM and AFDM: A Resource-Matched Performance Comparison
summary: As a waveform candidate for next-generation wireless systems, affine frequency division multiplexing (AFDM) has often been compared with orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) under different configurations, while a systematic comparison of their pilot-based sensing performance remains lacking. This paper establishes a comparison with the same bandwidth, frame duration, pilot energy, and reserved-resource overhead. OFDM-random, OFDM-fixed-comb, and OFDM-shifted-comb pilots are compared with AFDM pilots surrounded by guard resources using aperiodic ambiguity functions without cyclic prefix/chirp-periodic prefix (CP/CPP) and cyclic ambiguity functions with CP/CPP, followed by target detection experiments. The results show that OFDM-fixed-comb exhibits low range sidelobes but periodic range ambiguity peaks, while AFDM and OFDM-shifted-comb effectively suppress zero-Doppler range ambiguities. Within the common unambiguous region, all pilot configurations for both waveforms exhibit similar detection thresholds in strong-target detection, while structured OFDM and AFDM pilot placements outperform OFDM-random in weak-target detection. At high mobility, the AFDM receiver using the discrete affine Fourier transform (DAFT) can resolve integer Doppler beyond the conventional slow-time maximum unambiguous velocity, outperforming the tested conventional OFDM and AFDM receivers at the increased search complexity. These results separate the effects of waveform, pilot placement, and receiver processing, providing a basis for AFDM and OFDM pilot-based sensing design.

title: Parametric Resonance in Primal-Dual Learning for Slowly Non-Stationary Constrained MDPs
summary: Primal-dual methods for constrained Markov decision processes are analyzed under a two-timescale assumption, with non-stationarity entering through two channels. In the additive channel, where the constraint level oscillates, the dual oscillation saturates at a floor set by the moving optimum and is amplified linearly by the timescale ratio. In the parametric channel, where the constraint sensitivity oscillates, a coherent modulation carries no resonant forcing at any depth: the dual update's stiffness modulation cancels the primal update's damping modulation. Instability instead comes from a mismatch between the constraint estimate used by the primal update and the measurement used by the dual update, producing a parametric resonance at twice the pair's natural frequency. The tolerated mismatch grows with the square root of the forcing bandwidth and collapses with the square root of the dual-to-primal step-size ratio. These results hold on the tangent linear-quadratic reduction around an active saddle, for one constraint and for $K$ constraints under a common modulation and an isotropy condition. Driving both updates from the same estimate removes the resonant forcing but introduces a stationary offset equal to the estimator's bias. In a Lagrangian soft actor-critic agent, the multiplier locks onto the sub-harmonic at the timescale ratios its identified linear loop predicts and a coherent cost critic suppresses the lock-in, while a proportional (PID) term, predicted to leave the lock-in in place, suppresses most of it through the projection of the multiplier.

title: Trust but Verify: Designing Region-Inhomogeneous Forward Dynamics for Discrete Diffusion
comment: Accepted to 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: AI for Stochastic Dynamics. 10 pages
summary: Continuous diffusion treats the forward process as a design space; discrete language diffusion often uses absorbing corruption, leaving context fully trusted throughout generation. This makes trust binary: corrupted context is copied as ground truth, propagating errors into generated spans. We reopen this design space by combining absorbing and uniform-mixing kernels with region-dependent rates. Missing positions follow absorbing dynamics, while context undergoes low-rate random substitution, exposing the model to observed but uncertain tokens during training. At inference, a heuristic sampler re-injects noise into suspicious context under an annealed intensity and freezes context updates late in the trajectory. An 8,000-step finetune of a pretrained 170M-parameter masked diffusion model takes under five hours on a 6 GB laptop GPU. The base model assigns roughly 50% probability to observed tokens even when they are uniform-random garbage. For uniform-random corruption, finetuning detects corrupted context with 0.96 recall and 0.91 precision, improves infill token-F1 by 3.8 points at 10% corruption and 6.4 points at 20%, and removes the accuracy dip next to corruptions. Clean conditioning shows no measurable regression, with a false-edit rate below 0.4%. Gains for plausible corruptions are weaker: about 0.5 F1 points at 10% corruption, without statistical significance. Our results suggest that detectability and damage depend jointly on departure from the data conditional: nearby noise is hard to detect and semantically mild, while distant noise is conspicuous and destructive. We interpret absorbing diffusion as the infinite-contrast limit of a trust axis, analogous to the signal-to-noise gap between known and unknown regions in diffusion inpainting. In our setting of a 170M model and a single text domain, intermediate trust is reached by changing forward dynamics rather than architecture.

title: Temporal vs Spectral Resolution in CSI Reporting for Wi-Fi ISAC
summary: CSI feedback is fundamental to proposed uses of Wi-Fi sensing such as human activity recognition (HAR); but it also constitutes significant overhead as resources must be allocated away from data communications. Wi-Fi CSI extraction can be explored along two dimensions in IEEE 802.11bf: reporting intensity, i.e., temporal resolution, and number of reported subcarriers, i.e., spectral resolution. We explore periodic and IEEE 802.11bf threshold-based reporting at matched rates, and uniform decimation and block-mean grouping at matched report sizes. We further propose reporting the mean CSI accumulated since the last report. Using the 802.11bf report size as the metric, we evaluate the accuracy-cost tradeoffs on three public datasets with our proposed model, a convolutional neural network combined with a gated recurrent unit and temporal pyramid pooling. The proposed periodic reporting with mean payload and block-mean grouping improves accuracy by up to 53 percentage points at equal CSI overhead cost. Temporal resolution is generally more cost-effective than spectral resolution. With only at most 7.7% of full-CSI feedback cost, the proposed scheme achieves 96-98% of full-CSI accuracy.

title: Efficient spectral unmixing using endmember variability
summary: A mixed signal vector composed of a weighted sum of random, unobserved endmember vectors has a mean and a variance that both depend on the unknown weights. This suggests that linear estimates of the weights based on the mean model are likely to be inefficient, and could possibly be improved upon by estimates that also make use of the variance model. In the context of a latent factor model for source variability, we calculate theoretically how much information is available in the variance model, and show how this information may stabilize inference in the case of an ill-conditioned mean model. We show through several data examples that utilization of the variance model is likely to improve parameter estimation in real-world scenarios.

title: Binding-Specific Relearning Savings for Test-Time Continual Learning
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Towards Test-Time Continual Learning Agents (TTCL). 15 pages, 2 figures. Code: https://github.com/zhezhou1106/relearning-savings
summary: When a fact becomes harder to elicit from a language model, has the model lost it, or has it merely become less accessible? Parameter-updating test-time continual learning agents are usually evaluated by current output accuracy; we ask whether that measurement captures how prior experience shapes later updates. We test whether learning a specific factual binding produces a later relearning advantage beyond familiarity with its entity, answer vocabulary, format, or query slot. In Qwen2.5-1.5B, we compare three matched, counterbalanced histories: LEARNED receives the correct binding, CONTROL receives matched exposure without it, and WRONG receives a competing relation-valid answer in the same slot. After an identical rehearsal-free continual fine-tuning stream, LEARNED reacquires the target faster than CONTROL at a prespecified checkpoint of partial forgetting. WRONG shows no positive advantage over CONTROL, while its comparison with LEARNED provides slot-matched corroboration, subject to possible competitor interference. The advantage remains positive after adjustment for measured pre-relearning behavior. In a secondary descriptive conversion using an unpaired never-seen pool, prior learning reduces the optimizer updates required for restoration by about 18%. Current behavioral accuracy can therefore underestimate the lasting effect of previously acquired experience. Code is available at https://github.com/zhezhou1106/relearning-savings

title: Sensing-Driven Secure Transmission with Mobile Eavesdropper Tracking in RIS-Assisted ISAC
summary: The mobility of potential eavesdroppers (Eves) poses a critical challenge to physical-layer security (PLS) in integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems, since rapidly varying Eve positions lead to time-varying eavesdropping channels and outdated security decisions. To address this challenge, this paper investigates sensing-driven secure transmission for reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted ISAC systems with a maneuvering Eve. To this end, by exploiting the dual functionality of the ISAC waveform, a multi-view angle estimation method jointly exploiting the base station (BS) and RIS is developed based on MUSIC and maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), enabling three-dimensional (3D) Eve localization, whose accuracy is characterized by the Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB). Subsequently, an interacting multiple model extended Kalman filter (IMM-EKF) with out-of-sequence measurement (OOSM) compensation is employed to track and predict the maneuvering Eve. Based on the predicted trajectory, the time-varying eavesdropping channel is updated, and the transmit beamforming and RIS phase shifts are jointly optimized subject to a sensing CRLB constraint. Furthermore, an alternating optimization (AO) algorithm integrating fractional programming, semidefinite relaxation (SDR), and Riemannian manifold optimization is developed to solve the resulting non-convex problem. Finally, numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in accurately tracking maneuvering Eves and enhancing secure transmission in dynamic ISAC environments.

title: Task-aware Kernel Stein certificates for Rényi differential privacy
summary: Rènyi differential privacy, based on Rènyi divergence, has become a notion of choice for privacy guarantees. However, outside the Gaussian setting, Rènyi divergence can be difficult to compute. In particular, Rènyi differential privacy guarantees that exploit task-specific information, as in Rènyi Pufferfish privacy, can be challenging. Here we use kernel Stein discrepancies based on escort distributions to provide certificates for Rènyi differential privacy. By designing the kernel to focus on the relevant privacy directions, we also derive task-aware privacy certificates. We provide exact identities for Gaussian and Laplace mechanisms and bounds for exponential mechanisms, with separate task-aware guarantees. A real data set example illustrates how the protected comparison set and the released subspace jointly determine the resulting certificates.

title: Eliciting Specifications: When Does Interactive Clarification Help?
comment: Accepted to NeurIPs 2026 Workshop on AI for Verifiable Coding
summary: LLMs can generate Lean specifications from task descriptions, but those descriptions are often underspecified or ambiguous and may omit verifier-relevant edge cases, yielding imperfect formal specifications. We study whether an elicitation agent (EA) can improve verifier-checked Lean specifications by seeking clarification from a reference-grounded simulated developer before formalization. The agent decomposes the task, identifies unresolved decisions, asks bounded clarification questions, and uses the answers to write a refined natural-language specification that an LLM formalizer then translates into Lean. On 189 Verina Lean 4 specification-generation tasks, we compare single-shot generation with elicitation under question budgets of k=3 and k=10, allowing at most three or ten EA questions per task, across same-model and cross-model configurations. The same-model Claude Sonnet 4.6 pipeline has negative strict pass@1 estimates at both budgets, showing elicitation is not a uniform accuracy booster. In contrast, the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 and Sonnet 4.6-to-Gemini 3.8 Flash pipelines have positive strict estimates. The largest strict result reaches 65.6%, a +6.3-point change (+12 tasks), in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 pipeline. Six of eight conditions have positive compile-conditional estimates, with a maximum cross-model difference of +4.9 points among compiling outputs. Treatment estimates also differ across the basic and advanced splits; the largest advanced-task change occurs in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 configuration at k=10, from 42.0% to 50.6%. Failure analysis identifies postconditions as the largest source of degradation. These findings suggest future autoformalization systems should treat elicited natural-language specifications as intermediate artifacts and optimize jointly for semantic correctness among compiling outputs and reliable translation of clarified information into Lean.

title: A Smaller Subspace is All You Need: Efficient ISAC Beamforming via Dimensionality Reduction
summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) has been recognized as a critical technology for the sixth generation (6G) wireless networks. Under monostatic sensing mode, achieving a balance between communication and sensing performance via optimal beamforming is a critical research problem. In multiple input multiple output (MIMO) systems, such beamforming problems are of substantial computational complexity due to the large number of antennas. Existing methods exploit exact subspaces of lower dimensions to speed up the beamforming process where the complexity is proportional to the number of communication users and sensing targets instead of antennas. In this paper, it is demonstrated that the beamforming problem can be solved in an even lower-dimensional subspace with only a small sensing performance loss. Numerical results compare the sensing performance and computational complexity of ISAC beamforming problem in the exact subspace and smaller subspaces.

title: Learning without relearning physical symmetry: an SO(3)-equivariant convolutional network (CNN) on the sphere
summary: Many of the most important datasets in the physical sciences live natively on the sphere, and these data often carry no preferred position or orientation. Using methods that do not reflect this symmetry leads to far higher simulation requirements, which can be catastrophic for scientific analyses (forcing reliance on cheap, imperfect models that bias results). We present a novel spherical implementation of a gauge equivariant mesh architecture that is specifically designed for the Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization (\healpix{}) of the sphere. The $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-equivariant convolution is built from steerable filters, parallel transport and spin-weighted features. The architecture supplies the exact symmetry, so the network does not spend training data learning it. The convolution operations are constructed to give provably exact equivariance, given a band-limit. Our full CNNs can achieve SO(3)-invariance error at per-cent-level and lower, which is controlled through well-understood hyperparameters. On benchmarks, our technique gives the most accurate dense gradient regression and competitive cosmic microwave background foreground removal and denoising. The improved simulation efficiency matters most in simulation-based inference (SBI), where high-fidelity simulations are expensive and neural compressors require large training sets, so a fixed budget forces analyses with less accurate simulators. In cosmology lensing SBI, our technique yields the tightest posteriors at matched simulation count. This approach is a novel method that will enable new convolutional neural network analyses, including generative and inference tasks, for processes and data on the sphere.

title: Not All Frames Are Equal:Difference-Aware Quantization for Ultra-Low-Bit ASR
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at Interspeech 2026
summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) methods such as GPTQ and AWQ compress large language models effectively, but applying them to automatic speech recognition (ASR) at ultra-low bit-widths (2-3 bits) causes severe transcription degradation. Unlike discrete text tokens, speech activations are highly correlated in steady-state and zero-padded regions yet change rapidly at phonetic boundaries; when all frames contribute equally to the Hessian, static frames dominate calibration and obscure informative transitions. We propose DiffAQ, which computes frame-to-frame activation differences to measure the rate of acoustic change and assigns Hessian importance proportionally, concentrating quantization precision on phonetically critical frames. As a training-free modification to GPTQ, DiffAQ consistently reduces WER across various Whisper sizes and standard benchmarks, with the largest gains at 2-bit precision where baseline methods frequently produce degenerate outputs.

title: Diversifying Moving Target Defense Against Adaptive Attacks Through Factorized Diffusion
summary: Proactive defense offers a means to enhance power-system cybersecurity through controlled modifications of system configurations. One example is moving target defense (MTD), which uses distributed flexible AC transmission system (D-FACTS) devices to perturb transmission-line reactances against stealthy false data injection attacks. Existing MTD methods primarily rely on deterministic optimization, producing a single perturbation plan for each operating condition. However, repeated or highly correlated plans may expose predictable system configurations that attackers can learn and exploit. To address this limitation, this paper reformulates MTD as a conditional generative problem that produces diverse, secure, and physically feasible perturbation candidates. Learning such a distribution is challenging because MTD decisions jointly involve selecting branches, determining perturbation magnitudes, and coordinating adjustments across the network. To make this problem tractable, we factorize the decision distribution into three sequential conditional stages: branch selection, magnitude allocation, and continuous refinement. Graph-conditioned diffusion models are employed to capture the discrete and continuous decisions while accounting for network dependencies. Furthermore, a - objective is incorporated into diffusion training to favor candidates with desirable defense effectiveness and operational costs. Numerical studies on the IEEE 118- and 300-bus systems show that the proposed framework achieves AC feasibility comparable to that of optimization-based MTD baselines and higher - values, while reducing online computation time by an order of magnitude. The generated candidate pool remains effective under changing operating conditions and device availability, providing diverse high-value alternatives for flexible online cyber defense.

title: ENFR: Evidence Networks with Flow-Matched References for Amortized Simulation-Based Model Inference
summary: The evidence, $\mathcal{Z} = p(x | \mathcal{M})$, of a data-generating model $\mathcal{M}$ is a powerful tool in Bayesian frameworks: it enables model inference, model misspecification tests, and goodness-of-fit assessment as an alternative to standard discrepancy statistics, e.g. $χ^2$. While versatile, the evidence is notoriously difficult to compute, even when the likelihood is available. In both likelihood-based and simulation-based inference, estimating $\mathcal{Z}$ provides an immediate solution to high-dimensional goodness-of-fit or model misspecification tests: using $\mathcal{Z}(x)$ as the test statistic induces a minimum-volume level-$α$ test. Such tests are essential to assess model fidelity, which is necessary to trust simulation-based parameter inference. Existing learned approaches largely target Bayes factors, which only measure evidence ratios. Instead, we provide accurate, fast, and amortized estimates of the absolute evidence. We present ENFR: Evidence Networks with Flow-matched References. Building on the Evidence Network framework of Jeffrey & Wandelt (2024), the proposed method first learns Bayes factors with respect to a flow-matched reference, from which the absolute evidence is recovered. We show improvement in estimation of $\mathcal{Z}$ over the flow-based baseline in all applications considered and the best performance of all density estimation methods considered in our benchmarks. We furthermore introduce and provide the proof for an architecture that jointly learns the individual evidences of a set of models $\{\mathcal{M}_i\}$. We demonstrate the performance and scaling behavior of these approaches on data from a variety of scientific applications.

title: When the implementation matters more than the algorithm: NSGA-II and other multi-objective optimizers in engineering design tools
comment: 29 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables. Per-run data, emulator models and analysis scripts: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23157761
summary: Engineering design tools increasingly embed optimizers as ready-made components that users select by algorithm name, while operator settings and bound, integer and duplicate handling stay fixed inside each tool. This study tests whether the name predicts the result. A tool-agnostic harness exposes one deterministic black box, an emulator of a published 22-variable mixed-integer building-performance problem, to the native optimizers of three Grasshopper plug-ins, to canonical NSGA-II, SMS-EMOA and GDE3 from Python libraries, and to the model-based RBFMOpt. Eighteen configurations were run at 5,000 evaluations under three population allocations, with statistics fixed in advance. Four NSGA-II implementations differed by up to 5% in hypervolume, more than three canonical algorithms of different families differed from one another, and their response to population size differed by up to 10 percentage points; for two MOEA/D implementations, by 28. On ZDT test functions the same NSGA-II implementations differed up to 470-fold in IGD. An ablation in one open-source NSGA-II reproduced the behaviour of one tool from its documented settings but not the gaps of the other two, so documented parameters do not identify an implementation. Counting the budget in wall-clock time reversed the ranking of the model-based optimizer, and reporting the final population instead of the archive understated some configurations by up to a third; most differences fell below the surrogate's error. For optimizers embedded in design-support systems, the implementation is part of the method; a reporting checklist is derived: implementation and version, effective settings, budget in time and evaluations, and archive-based indicators.

title: QIEN: Quantum-Inspired Energy-Neutral UAV Trajectory for WPT-Enabled Industrial HRLLC
comment: 14 pages. Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Vehicular Technology. This work was supported by the Postdoctoral Research Fellowship from the Fonds de recherche du Québec (FRQ) under Grant 368613
summary: This paper introduces Quantum-Inspired Energy-Neutral (QIEN) UAV Trajectory for WPT-Enabled Industrial HRLLC, a novel framework for mobility-integrated trajectory and resource optimization in solar-powered uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) relay systems supporting autonomous mining robots in post-disaster environments. We formulate a mixed-integer nonlinear program (MINLP) that jointly optimizes UAV trajectory, finite blocklength allocation, transmit power, and wireless power transfer (WPT) over discrete time horizons to maximize aggregate data throughput. The system operates under strict extreme hyper-reliable low-latency communication (HRLLC) constraints, energy sustainability requirements via solar harvesting, and continuous robot power delivery. To solve this large-scale optimization problem, QIEN employs a hybrid Cooperative Quantum-behaved Particle Swarm Optimization (Co-QPSO) algorithm using quantum tunneling mechanisms and a heterogeneous swarm architecture. Our simulation results demonstrate that the proposed QIEN framework significantly outperforms benchmark algorithms, achieving successful convergence while maintaining energy-neutral operation and satisfying all reliability, power, and mobility constraints.

title: Canonical Layer Inference for Deep Gaussian Processes via Symmetry-Breaking Augmentation
summary: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are flexible priors for compositional regression functions, but inference for intermediate layers faces questions. The basic obstruction is an adjacent-layer symmetry: applying an invertible transformation and its inverse to two adjacent layers leaves the composed regression map unchanged. Under explicit symmetry and prior-comparability conditions, we show that the posterior may not concentrate on any prescribed intermediate-layer representation, even when the composed regression function is estimable. We then introduce an augmented $ρ$-fractional posterior that reweights layer decompositions by a non-saturating identity-deviation penalty. The augmentation changes posterior odds between symmetry-related decompositions by an exponential penalty ratio. Under proper choices of the penalty and a prior mass condition, it preserves function-level fractional posterior contraction, while shrinking the redundant layers towards the identity mapping. Thus, the likelihood does not identify a unique ``true'' set of layers; the augmentation favors identity-biased parsimonious decompositions within an equivalence class of layers; uniqueness of a selected representative is not established.

title: Rethinking User Encoders: Routing Diffusion States for Scenario-Adaptive User Representation
summary: Existing large language model (LLM)-based user encoders serialize heterogeneous behavioral logs and compress them into static representations through autoregressive (AR) prediction. However, their unidirectional constraint limits bidirectional information flow, hindering cross-modal interactions and the joint preservation of multi-source signals. Consequently, the learned static representations struggle to accommodate the distinct evidence requirements of diverse downstream scenarios. We address these limitations by unlocking the iterative denoising process of diffusion language models (dLLMs) as a multi-granularity reconstruction space. Based on this insight, we propose FINDERS (FactorIzatioN of Diffusion statEs for Routing across Scenarios), a router-equipped dLLM framework comprising four operations: denoise, factorize, route, and compress. Learnable meta-slots organize complementary denoising states into transferable cross-modal semantics and modality-specific behavioral factors. To provide grounded supervision, we construct BehaviorQA, a large-scale corpus containing explicit behavioral rationales. Guided by scenario queries, a lightweight router dynamically emphasizes relevant slot directions via an input-level residual pathway before cross-source fusion and final compression. Extensive experiments and online A/B tests across ten industrial scenarios demonstrate that FINDERS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both unified and scenario-adaptive settings. This work effectively pushes the boundaries of dLLMs beyond language generation, demonstrating their immense potential as powerful user representation learners.

title: Exploiting the Flexibility of LLM Inference for Frequency Regulation Service
summary: While the widespread deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly driven up power demands in computing clusters, the unique execution characteristics of LLM inference offer a novel opportunity to utilize these clusters as controllable loads. In this paper, we investigate the potential of LLM inference cluster to provide frequency regulation services through inference request scheduling. First, we model the problem as a hierarchical Markov decision process that includes request-to-replica dispatching and token-level resource allocation. Then, we introduce a reward redistribution network to address the temporal asynchrony between millisecond-level scheduling decisions and second-level frequency regulation signals. Furthermore, we develop an optimization framework based on a mean-field approximation to enable coordination among a large number of replicas under high request concurrency. Simulations using real-world data demonstrate that the proposed approach accurately tracks frequency regulation signals without compromising service-level objectives.

title: Identifiability from Moments in Independent Component Analysis Mixture Models
summary: We study Independent Component Analysis (ICA) mixture models. These models consist of mixtures of ICA densities. An ICA density is associated with a random vector whose coordinates become mutually independent after an invertible linear transformation. ICA mixture models are nonparametric extensions of the celebrated family of Gaussian mixtures. We show that in many cases the ICA mixtures are identifiable from the collection of the observed moment tensors, that is, the mixing coefficients, linear transformations, and source moments of order up to $d$ can be identified from the moment tensors of order up to $d$ for generic parameters. We address the problem by studying the corresponding secant varieties and their algebraic properties such as dimensions and Gauss maps. In particular, for $n$-variate distributions, we establish that generically and up to the trivial scaling and permutation symmetries, when $d\geq 5$, the parameters can be recovered uniquely for asymptotically up to $n^{d-2}/d!$ mixture components. For $d=3,4$, we show identifiability up to a finite equivalence class for asymptotically up to $n^{d-2}/d!$ and $0.5 n^{d-2}/d!$ components respectively, where for $d=4$ the mixing coefficients need to be known a priori. The obtained bounds on the component numbers have the maximum possible orders in $n$, and for $d = 3$ and $d\geq 5$, they are also asymptotically sharp.

title: Audio System One Model: Typed Probabilistic Perception of Emotion in Speech
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to ICASSP2027
summary: Speech applications ask many questions about the same voice: which emotion a listener perceives, how aroused the speaker sounds, whether they sound frustrated. Classifiers answer fast, over one fixed label set; audio language models (ALMs) take any question in text, but answer by generation, one pass per question, with poorly calibrated probabilities.
